cards.explanation: The people grumble against Moses. He's Israel's leader, and they ask him, “What are we to drink?” (Exodus 15:24). Three days of walking with no water will do that to a crowd. I think I'd be asking somebody that question too, and I'd be loud about it.

Moses cries out to the LORD. He doesn't answer the grumbling with a speech, and the LORD shows him a log (Exodus 15:25). I love that order, because he goes to the right place first. Take it from a stamper who spent years in a drawer: when you're stuck, start there.

The word is sweet. Moses cast the log into the waters, and “…they were sweetened.” (Exodus 15:25). The LORD was the one who showed him that log, so Moses didn't have to guess. After three days of walking without finding water, I think that was a big relief.

The word is diseases. The LORD says, “…then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians.” (Exodus 15:26). The promise comes with an if, because He's asking them to listen carefully, do what is right in His eyes, and keep His commands. It's a promise worth holding onto.
The answer is True. The LORD says, “For I am the LORD who heals you.” (Exodus 15:26). He says it right there at the water He just sweetened. I'd say that's a good place to hear it.

At Elim they find twelve springs and seventy palm trees. The text says there were “…twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees…” and the people camped there by the waters (Exodus 15:27). Water and shade, right after all that dry walking. I think that camp felt like a vacation.

They say they had pots of meat and plenty of bread. “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread…” (Exodus 16:3). Notice what they remember: the meals. I think hunger has a way of making the past look like a buffet.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day.” (Exodus 16:4). Nobody is told to haul in a week's worth at once. The one change comes on the sixth day, when what they bring in is twice as much (Exodus 16:5).

The LORD sets it up to test whether they will follow His instructions. He says, “In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions.” (Exodus 16:4). The daily gathering is how that test works. The text states the reason itself, so we don't have to guess.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “Then on the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days.” (Exodus 16:5). So the sixth day has a double portion built in. Hold onto that detail, because it matters later.

The answer is the LORD. Moses says, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.” (Exodus 16:8). He and Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), are just the ones standing in front of the crowd. He also asks, “…who are we…”, which sounds like a man who knows he's only the messenger.

The glory of the LORD appears in a cloud. The people look toward the desert, “…and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared.” (Exodus 16:10). It happens while Aaron is speaking to the whole congregation. I bet that was one fast turn of the head.

The answer is quail. “That evening quail came and covered the camp…” (Exodus 16:13). Moses had said the LORD would give them meat that evening (Exodus 16:8), and the evening is when it shows up. Covered the camp, friends. I think that's a whole lot of birds.

They ask one another, “What is it?” They ask it because “…they did not know what it was.” (Exodus 16:15). Then Moses tells them it's the bread the LORD has given them to eat. They had no idea what they were looking at, and I think that's a fair reaction.

The answer is True. When they measured it by the omer, “…he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.” (Exodus 16:18). Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat. I think it's wonderful that the one who gathered little came up with no shortfall.
The answer is False. The text says, “…they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning…” (Exodus 16:20). So not everyone listened. That's how the maggots enter the story.

The leftover bread gets maggots and starts to smell. The text says it “…became infested with maggots and began to smell.” (Exodus 16:20). That was the part they kept after Moses said not to. I've forgotten a batch on the counter, but never one like that.

The answer is True. “Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.” (Exodus 16:21). So the bread is only there to gather until the sun gets hot. That's a deadline with no snooze button. You can't hit it once and roll over for ten more minutes, because the sun doesn't care how you slept.

Moses says tomorrow is a day of complete rest. “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.” (Exodus 16:23). The double portion on the sixth day sets it up. The people get a day to rest, and the bread is already covered.

The answer is True. “So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots.” (Exodus 16:24). Same overnight wait as before, and a totally different morning. Earlier, the leftovers had maggots and began to smell (Exodus 16:20). I leave one batch out and it's a mess, but I think the secret here is that the LORD told them to.

Moses says the bread won't be there on the seventh day. He says, “For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there.” (Exodus 16:26). So there's no reason to go looking. I think he's telling them the field will be empty.

The word is stay. The LORD says, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.” (Exodus 16:29). He says this right after telling them He has given them the Sabbath. Stay put, friends.

The manna is kept so future generations can see it. The LORD commanded, “Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 16:32). The manna is kept so those who come later can see it. That's a good thing to put in a jar.

The answer is years. “The Israelites ate manna forty years…” (Exodus 16:35), until they reached the border of Canaan. That's forty years of the LORD's bread, and nobody ever had to check a tracking number. I think that's a lot of mornings, friends.
